conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mrs. ___. I’m Dr. ___, part of your care team. You’re here today for your scheduled surgery on your thoracic spine—specifically, a discectomy at T3-4 and T6-7 levels. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit nervous, to be honest. The back pain’s been constant, but I’m hoping this helps. I’ve had so many procedures already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I completely understand. Given your history—especially the lymphoma and immune deficiency—we’ve taken extra precautions. Your surgery is planned as a transpedicular discectomy, which means we’ll remove the disc material pressing on your nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay during the surgery? I remember last time my platelets were low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we checked your labs this morning. Your platelet count was 108, which is on the lower side, so you’ll receive two units of platelets before surgery to reduce bleeding risk. Everything else looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. And my diabetes and asthma—are they under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar is within target range, and your asthma is stable. We’ll continue your inhalers as needed. You’re on prophylactic acyclovir too, given your history of oral herpes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my methadone—I take it four times a day for chronic pain. Will that continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll manage your pain with your usual methadone and add hydromorphone for breakthrough pain after surgery. But we’ll avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen for two weeks to protect healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No Advil. I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll also start you on pantoprazole to protect your stomach, especially with the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in—you’ve received the platelets and are prepped. Surgery is scheduled for noon. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Just hope it helps the pain and doesn’t cause new problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. The goal is to relieve nerve pressure and improve your function. You’ll wake up in the PACU, and I’ll see you later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mrs. ___, you’re back on the floor. The surgery went well—T3-4 and T6-7 discectomies completed without complications. You were extubated in the PACU and are doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. I’m groggy, but I can move my legs. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your strength is intact, which is excellent. We’ll keep you on oxygen for now and monitor your pain. You’re on IV hydromorphone, but we’ll switch to oral soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with ice chips and advance your diet slowly. Given your colostomy history, we’ll watch for any bowel issues, but so far, everything looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. On post-op day one, your exam is stable. Pain is controlled with oral meds. We’ve advanced your diet to clear liquids—you tolerated them well overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My back feels sore, but not worse than before. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, expected soreness. The surgical pain should improve over the next few days. We’ll keep you on acetaminophen and hydromorphone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like metformin and levothyroxine—am I taking those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you resumed all home medications this morning—metformin, levothyroxine, methadone, and your inhalers. We added docusate and senna to prevent constipation from the narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve had bad constipation before with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re staying ahead of it. You’ll also get IVIG every three weeks as usual—your immune deficiency means we need to be cautious about infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s post-op day two. We removed your Foley catheter this morning—you voided without issues, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no problem. But last night, I felt short of breath for a bit. My oxygen dropped, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw a brief drop in your oxygen saturation. Your lung exam was clear, and the chest X-ray showed no pneumonia or pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it the pain medicine? I’ve had reactions before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think so. The IV hydromorphone can suppress breathing. We’ve discontinued the IV dose and are sticking to oral meds only as needed. Your oxygen is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t something serious. My asthma hasn’t acted up, has it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lungs are clear. The chest X-ray confirmed no fluid or infection. We’ll keep your albuterol available just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology report is back—your chest X-ray is normal. Heart size, lungs, and pleura are all clear. No signs of complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So, can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. A home health nurse and physical therapist will visit you daily at first. You’ll need help with stairs and lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mom’s helping. But how will I manage the pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have hydrocodone for breakthrough pain, acetaminophen, and your regular methadone. Take them as directed. Don’t wait until the pain is severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the staples—how long until they come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about two weeks. Until then, keep the incision clean and dry. No baths or swimming. Have someone check it daily for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And when do I see you again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the office in a few days to schedule your follow-up. We’ll assess healing, remove staples, and discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—afebrile, stable vitals, moving at your baseline. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m ready to go home. Just nervous about managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. You’ll have nursing and PT support. Take it slow—no lifting over 10 pounds, no twisting. Use your walker as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your pain meds. But call us if pain isn’t controlled, or if you develop fever, weakness, numbness, or bowel/bladder issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my lymphoma—any concern it came back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of recurrence. You’re still in remission. Continue your follow-ups with oncology as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send your discharge instructions and meds. Your mother will help you settle in. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—your discharge meds are ready. You’ve got hydrocodone, acetaminophen, docusate, senna, and all your regulars like metformin and levothyroxine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the methadone included? I need it four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, methadone 5 mg four times daily is on the list. And acyclovir for herpes prevention, loratadine for allergies, and duloxetine for nerve pain and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to run out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We made sure everything’s covered. You’re cleared to go home with services. Take it easy, and follow up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your discharge paperwork is complete. You’re officially discharged as of now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go.
